title: The Last Page: Puja in the Heart
hookLine: the shrine is packed in a box: what's left of worship?
carry: puja is the heart settled, not only the flowers
tomorrow: why would anyone offer flowers to a drawing of triangles?

lines: THE SHRINE IS IN A BOX.
cards: A move scatters a life into boxes labeled kitchen and misc. Somewhere in one of them is the small home shrine: the brass lamp, the bell, the little images wrapped in newspaper.

For someone whose morning starts with a lamp and a flower, a week without that corner can feel like a week off balance. So yesterday's question gets sharper. If the flowers are packed, what's left of worship?
The Vijnana Bhairava's closing verses take that question head on.

teach.h: DHYANA: A STEADY MIND, NO SHAPE.
teach.b: Near its end, the book picks up three familiar words and turns each one over. Dhyana, meditation, it says, isn't picturing a god with a body, arms and a face.
It's a mind become steady, resting without a made-up shape to hold. Puja, worship, isn't the offering of flowers.
It's the heart settled, with care, in the vast openness beyond thought. And the fire offering? What goes into the flames is the mind's own scattering, offered into the fire of awareness.
One careful way to read this: it isn't mocking flowers or fire, and it never tells anyone to stop lighting the lamp. It's naming what, in its view, the flowers and the fire point to.

teach.h: MANASA PUJA: WORSHIP IN THE MIND.
teach.b: Hindus have a name for worship done this way: manasa puja, worship in the mind, offering the lamp, the water and the flowers in the heart.
A hymn tradition credits to Shankara, the Shiva Manasa Puja, does exactly that, one imagined offering at a time. Then the dialogue ends the way it began, with two people.
The Goddess, who opened the book asking what Bhairava really is, is filled with joy, and she embraces him. The one who asked and the one who answered meet.
So here's what this book hands anyone whose shrine is still in a box: worship was never only on the shelf. The lamp will come out of the newspaper soon enough.
Meanwhile, the heart can settle anywhere.

how: Many who study the Vijnana Bhairava keep their outward worship, the lamp, the flowers, the fire, and read the closing verses as naming what those acts point to: a mind steady and a heart settled.

o: a tantric book that ends by turning worship inward
a hymn sung while the lamp is waved before a god
a temple manual on which flowers to offer, and when

it never says stop; it names what the flowers point to: the heart settled in openness.

games.q: you're away on a trip and can't do the morning puja you're used to. what does the Vijnana Bhairava's last page offer?
o: worship as the heart settled in openness, which needs no shelf.
nothing: without the lamp and flowers, the day's worship is lost.
a rule to give up outward worship for good and only meditate.
games.why: the closing verses call puja the heart settled in the openness beyond thought. they don't throw out the lamp; they say worship isn't only on the shelf.

practice: Sit tall and let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up, the way hands look when they're offering something.
If you pray, offer in your mind what you'd set on a shrine, a lamp, a flower, a little water, one by one, the way manasa puja does.
If you don't, set down the scattered bits of the day, the errands and the worries, like small things laid in a fire. Then stay, steady and open, with nothing in your hands at all.

wordCard.voice: The Vijnana Bhairava: a book of doors that ends by turning worship inward, and with the Goddess's embrace.
